name: The Whiting-Turner Contracting Company
employees: ~5,000 salaried (2025), about 1,000 of them in the Baltimore area
summary: BOTTOM LINE UP FRONT: Whiting-Turner is the fifth-largest contractor in the United States at USD 14.68bn of 2025 revenue, and it is on the marquee data-centre jobs — one of the builders of Vantage's Lighthouse campus in Wisconsin, prime on two separate USD 600m Google data centres — but it slipped from fourth to fifth in the ENR 2026 Top 400 while every data-centre specialist around it climbed, because at 27% telecom revenue it participates in the boom rather than being carried by it. BACKGROUND. Founded 1909 in Baltimore by G.W.C. Whiting and LeBaron Turner, MIT classmates; no relation to Turner Construction despite the surname. Privately held, with three chief executives in 115 years: the founders, Willard Hackerman (1955–2014, and sole stockholder during his tenure), and Timothy J. Regan since 2014. Construction management, general contracting, design-build and integrated project delivery across 24 declared market sectors and about 48 enumerated offices in 30 states, with no international revenue. It files nothing with the SEC, publishes no revenue figure of its own, and issued exactly one distributed press release in the trailing eighteen months. Collection gap: the widely repeated description of the company as employee-owned or an ESOP is unsupported — see the ownership judgment below.
ecosystemRole: Whiting-Turner is one of the small set of general contractors capable of taking a hyperscale data-hall building at gigawatt-campus scale, and it appears in this corpus mainly through the campuses it builds for others rather than through anything it owns. Its data-centre practice runs out of a Mission Critical business unit whose national leader also runs the in-house mechanical and electrical group — an organisational tell, since the company subcontracts every trade and holds its MEP expertise as a coordination and commissioning function rather than a self-perform division. It has documented substation, central-plant and combined-heat-and-power capability, but no battery storage, on-site generation or microgrid delivery appears anywhere in the public record; on the Lighthouse campus the utility scope sits with a specialist subcontractor rather than with Whiting-Turner. For the storage side of this corpus it is therefore a builder of the load, not of the power behind it.

productsAndServices.name: Mission critical — data centres
productsAndServices.description: One of 24 declared market sectors, and the one that has driven the company's growth. Delivered through a dedicated business unit whose national leader, Greg Botteon, also leads the in-house mechanical and electrical group — the two roles sitting with one person is the clearest available statement of how Whiting-Turner organises data-centre work.
highlights: One of the builders of Vantage Data Centers' Lighthouse campus at Port Washington, Wisconsin — a USD 15bn, 2.5 million square foot, four-building campus on 672 acres, with Oracle as operator and OpenAI as tenant under the Stargate programme.

Prime contractor on two separate Google data centres, each reported at about USD 600m: The Dalles / Wasco County, Oregon (290,000 sq ft, contracted through Google subsidiary Design LLC) and Clarksville, Tennessee.

Named data-centre projects on its own site are mostly confidential: an IBM B009 upgrade in Boulder (100,000 sq ft, live-facility UPS and generator replacement), a 54,000 sq ft confidential conversion in the Mountain States, and 'Project Oasis', a 465,000 sq ft server development and operations campus in the Southeast.
Ranked sixth in Building Design+Construction's 2025 data-centre contractor ranking, behind HITT, Holder, DPR, Clayco and Turner and ahead of Fortis, JE Dunn and Mortenson.

Stated technical concerns are conventional for the sector — redundancy, grounding, disaster recovery, PUE, commissioning, site hardening — with construction protocols for cleanliness, vibration and cable management.
productsAndServices.positioning: At 27% telecom revenue Whiting-Turner is a diversified general builder with a large data-centre line, not a mission-critical specialist. The contrast is the point: HITT runs 82% telecom, DPR 57%. Whiting-Turner outranks both overall while ranking below them in the sector.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Direct negotiated and construction-management-at-risk engagements with developers and hyperscalers; multi-contractor campus benches where it takes individual buildings alongside rivals.

productsAndServices.name: Construction management and general contracting
productsAndServices.description: The core business. Whiting-Turner describes itself as offering construction management, general contracting, design-build and integrated project delivery, and markets method selection rather than a method taxonomy — its own materials do not distinguish at-risk from agency construction management.
highlights: About 71% of 2025 revenue was construction-management-at-risk, per ENR's survey data; the same survey put it at 62% for 2022, so the mix has shifted toward at-risk delivery.
Sector mix 2025: 65% general building, 27% telecom, the remaining 8% across manufacturing, industrial and petroleum, and transportation. Zero international revenue.
Seven operating regions — Mid-Atlantic, Midwest, Mountain States, Northeast, Southeast, South Central and West.
The company states 'over 60 locations'; its own contact page enumerates about 48, the heaviest concentrations being California, Virginia, Texas, Pennsylvania and Florida.

Runs a materially higher share of hard-bid and lump-sum work than the data-centre specialists, which are at or near 100% at-risk — a lower-margin, higher-risk posture consistent with its heavy federal design-build book.
productsAndServices.positioning: Competes with Turner, HITT, Holder, DPR, Clayco, Fortis, JE Dunn, Mortenson, Clune, Hensel Phelps, Gilbane and Skanska USA. On the Lighthouse campus it works alongside three of them rather than against them — a multi-contractor campus is a co-opetition structure, and being one of the bench is itself the credential.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Direct negotiated work, competitive bid, and federal design-build under IDIQ vehicles.

productsAndServices.name: In-house MEP group and virtual design
productsAndServices.description: Whiting-Turner's stated technical differentiator, and worth reading precisely: the group provides mechanical and electrical review and coordination, not installation. Its listed services are preconstruction cost estimation, design review, long-lead equipment identification and procurement, trade contractor selection, testing and commissioning, BIM and constructability.
highlights: 'Trade contractor selection' among the group's own listed services is the tell — this is a coordination function layered over subcontracted trades.

No self-perform concrete, steel or MEP installation capability appears anywhere in the company's materials or in third-party reporting; peers that do self-perform publish dedicated pages for it and Whiting-Turner has none.
The entire trade base is subcontracted, with prequalification run through BuildingConnected.

Eight named practice areas alongside MEP: advanced delivery methods, high-performance buildings, lean, off-site construction, sustainability, virtual design and construction, and technology excellence.
Quality and safety are led by named executives — Kate Edwards on quality, Nadine Green on environmental health and safety — with OSHA 30-hour training for all operations personnel.
productsAndServices.positioning: For a data-centre client the relevant comparison is against contractors that self-perform MEP. Whiting-Turner's answer is coordination depth and commissioning rather than in-house trades, which is a genuinely different model and not obviously worse at campus scale.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Bundled into construction-management engagements rather than sold separately.

productsAndServices.name: Federal and military construction
productsAndServices.description: A smaller share of revenue than its visibility suggests, but the fastest-growing part of the book in this window and the one part of the business with hard, independently verifiable numbers, because federal awards are public.
highlights: 309 prime contract awards totalling USD 8.44bn across FY2008 to September 2026 per USASpending — Department of Defense USD 4.95bn, Department of Homeland Security USD 1.62bn, GSA USD 0.77bn, HHS USD 0.44bn.
At roughly USD 0.6–0.8bn a year against USD 14.7bn of total revenue, federal work is about 4–5% of the book. Whiting-Turner is overwhelmingly a private-client contractor.

May 2026: USD 516.7m of Coast Guard awards in a single announcement — up to USD 400m design-build at Training Center Cape May, New Jersey, described by the Coast Guard as the largest shore construction award in its history, plus USD 116.7m to recapitalise Pier Mike at Base Charleston.

September 2025: USD 137m for Base Seattle phase 1A, including dredging of contaminated sediment described as the largest CERCLA action in Coast Guard history, and about USD 69m for two membrane tension hangars at Air Station Barbers Point, Hawai'i.
Operates through joint ventures on some federal work — a Whiting-Turner Walsh JV appears in the federal recipient index and a Whiting-Turner Kokosing JV built the Amazon Air hub at Cincinnati.
productsAndServices.positioning: Federal design-build is where the company's lump-sum posture and its bonding relationships are exercised. Its standing surety panel — Liberty Mutual, Zurich American, and Fidelity and Deposit Company of Maryland — recurs across Miller Act actions in three courts over eight years.
productsAndServices.soldThrough: Competitive federal design-build and IDIQ delivery orders with NAVFAC, the Coast Guard, GSA and HHS.
targetSegments: Coast Guard and Navy shore infrastructure

strategyRead: 1. **(High confidence)** We assess Whiting-Turner participates in the data-centre boom rather than being carried by it, and that its own ENR submissions say so. Basis: revenue grew 10.4% in FY2025 against 11.8% for the Top 400 as a whole and 86.4% for the telecom category, and its rank fell from fourth to fifth in the same edition in which Mortenson rose twelve places, Clune thirteen and Fortis eleven, all on hyperscale books. At 27% telecom against HITT's 82% and DPR's 57% it is a diversified general builder with a large data-centre line. The climb is nonetheless real — the telecom share was roughly 9% three years earlier, implying growth from about USD 0.8bn to USD 4.0bn.

2. **(High confidence)** We assess the widely repeated claim that Whiting-Turner is employee-owned or operates an ESOP is unsupported and should not be carried. Basis: it does not appear on the National Center for Employee Ownership's Employee Ownership 100 while construction peers of identical size — McCarthy, JE Dunn, Swinerton, Sundt — all do; the company's own site never claims employee ownership, including on its careers pages; its press boilerplate omits it; and only a 401(k) profit-sharing plan surfaces in retirement-plan indexes. Every instance of the claim traces to a network of AI-generated content farms that also assert, on the same pages, that Willard Hackerman was sole stockholder — a mutually exclusive pair. What is supportable is that the firm is closely held, was wholly owned by Hackerman until his death in 2014, and that the disposition of that stake is unreported. Collection gap: a Department of Labor Form 5500 Schedule E would settle it and was unreachable from this session.

3. **(High confidence)** We assess Whiting-Turner is a pure construction manager that self-performs nothing, and that this is a deliberate model rather than a gap. Basis: its in-house MEP group lists trade contractor selection among its own services, alongside estimation, design review, procurement and commissioning — all coordination functions; its whole trade base is prequalified and subcontracted through BuildingConnected; and peers that do self-perform publish dedicated pages for it while Whiting-Turner has none. For a data-centre client this is the substantive difference between it and a self-perform rival.

4. **(Moderate confidence)** We assess the company's public silence is a deliberate posture with a measurable cost to outside assessment. Basis: it publishes no revenue, no backlog, no margin, no bonding capacity, no safety statistics and no ownership structure; three of the six data-centre projects on its own site are labelled confidential; it issued one distributed press release in eighteen months; it published nothing about the Lighthouse award while all three of its co-contractors did. Consequently almost everything hard in this dossier reaches the record because a counterparty was compelled to speak — ENR's survey, an EEOC consent decree, a Department of Labor debarment, USD 8.44bn of federal obligations, and a surety panel reconstructed from Miller Act party lists.

5. **(Moderate confidence)** We assess federal marine and installation work, not data centres, was the fastest-growing part of the book in this window. Basis: USD 516.7m of Coast Guard awards in a single May 2026 announcement including the largest shore construction award in that service's history, plus USD 137m at Base Seattle and about USD 69m in Hawai'i in late 2025, against a federal run-rate of USD 0.6–0.8bn a year. Federal work remains only 4–5% of revenue, so this shifts the growth story rather than the revenue mix.

6. **(Low confidence)** We assess Whiting-Turner has no battery storage, on-site generation or microgrid capability, and that this bounds its role in this corpus. Basis: four separate searches for storage, BESS or microgrid work returned nothing; what exists is conventional energy infrastructure — a campus substation and central plant at Stanford, a nominal 2 MW combined heat and power plant at Baltimore Washington Medical Center — and on Lighthouse the utility scope sits with Michels, a utility contractor, as subcontractor. Confidence is low rather than high only because a private contractor's scope is frequently invisible; the null is well controlled but a subcontracted storage scope would not necessarily surface.

policyExposure.exposure: On the NIH Building 10 East Wing renovation, where Whiting-Turner was the prime on a USD 181m contract, a second-tier subcontractor falsified certified payrolls to conceal paying below Davis-Bacon rates — sometimes more than 50% below — and denied overtime premiums to 22 workers. The Department of Labor recovered USD 531,173 for 45 ironworkers and debarred the subcontractor and two of its officers for three years. The first-tier subcontractor had failed to flow the required clauses down, and under 29 CFR 5.5(a)(6) the compliance obligation and the back-wage liability sit with the prime where flow-down fails.
policyExposure.mitigation: None disclosed publicly. The exposure is structural to being a prime on federally funded work with multiple subcontract tiers.

policyExposure.exposure: A USD 1.2m settlement and a two-year consent decree over conduct on the Clarksville, Tennessee Google data centre between May 2018 and autumn 2019 — segregated all-Black crews, racial slurs and graffiti, a noose displayed on Martin Luther King Jr.'s birthday, and the termination of two employees who complained. The decree required an explicit prohibition of hate symbols in the anti-harassment policy, an EEO liaison assigned to every construction site, and semi-annual Title VII training.
policyExposure.mitigation: The consent-decree obligations. Note that the company's navigation exposes a diversity and inclusion section whose pages return HTTP 404, and no supplier-diversity targets or workforce demographics are published — which is notable given the decree.

policyExposure.exposure: The University of Maryland Medical System and its affiliates paid Whiting-Turner at least USD 127m from 2012, including USD 89m for the 2013 Shock Trauma Center renovation, while chief executive Timothy J. Regan sat as vice chairman of the University of Maryland Medical Center board and a vice president sat on the St Joseph board. Both relationships were disclosed to state hospital regulators. The resulting legislation banned no-bid deals with board members, required full-board approval of member-company contracts, and forced sitting board members to resign — but did not extend to affiliates.
policyExposure.mitigation: Disclosure to regulators at the time; the statutory reform now governs the relationship. Recorded because a negotiated-work contractor's board relationships are exactly the kind of exposure a private company does not volunteer.

metrics.name: ENR Top 400 rank
metrics.result: Recorded as a miss on the sector rather than on the business: it added USD 1.4bn and still fell a place, because the Top 400 grew 11.8% and the telecom category grew 86.4% while it grew 10.4%. Kiewit passed it

metrics.name: Sector mix
metrics.actual: 65% general building, 27% telecom, 8% other; zero international
metrics.result: Against HITT at 82% telecom and DPR at 57%. The telecom share was roughly 9% three years earlier, implying growth from about USD 0.8bn to USD 4.0bn

metrics.name: Delivery mix
metrics.result: Up from 62% in FY2022, but still well below the data-centre specialists, which run at or near 100% at-risk — a higher share of hard-bid and lump-sum work than its peers

metrics.name: Federal prime awards
metrics.actual: About USD 0.6–0.8bn a year; USD 8.44bn cumulative across 309 awards since FY2008
metrics.result: From USASpending, which is authoritative and public — unlike everything else in this table. Roughly 4–5% of revenue

periods.commentary: No margin, no backlog, no bonding capacity, no leverage and no segment profitability is published, and none was obtainable. The company files nothing with the SEC, has no credit rating, and no private placement or debt facility surfaced. Its standing surety panel — Liberty Mutual, Zurich American, and Fidelity and Deposit Company of Maryland — was reconstructed from Miller Act party lists across three courts, which is the closest available proxy for financial capacity.

financials.commentary: Every revenue figure here reaches the record through ENR's confidential contractor survey. It is self-reported, unaudited and the single most load-bearing document in this dossier — the whole scale-and-trajectory picture rests on it. No analyst consensus exists or could exist for a private company with no public debt, so every 'expected' field is deliberately empty rather than manufactured. Two aggregator figures were rejected: a modelled USD 8.8bn 'in 2026' from a contact-data vendor, which is wrong by a wide margin, and a USD 4.3bn project pipeline dated 2017 whose headline project was never built.
